title: Ultralight (Part 103)
summary: Free ground school for pilots of single-seat ultralight vehicles under 14 CFR part 103: powered parachutes, paramotors, weight-shift trikes and light single-seat airplanes. No certificate is required, so this course teaches the rules, the airspace, the weather, the machines and the habits that keep you safe.
who: This course is for people who fly, or want to fly, ultralight vehicles under 14 CFR part 103: powered parachutes, paramotors, weight-shift trikes and single-seat ultralight airplanes. Part 103 has no pilot certificate, no medical, no knowledge test and no practical test, so nobody checks what you know. That makes your own study the whole safety system. The lessons use powered parachutes and paramotors as the main examples and cover trikes and fixed-wing ultralights where they differ. Learn the rules here, then fly with a qualified instructor.

facts.label: What counts as an ultralight vehicle
facts.value: One occupant, used for recreation or sport only, with no airworthiness certificate. Every item in 103.1 must be true, or Part 103 does not apply.

facts.label: Powered vehicle limits
facts.value: Empty weight under 254 pounds (floats and deployable safety devices are not counted), fuel capacity of 5 U.S. gallons or less, no more than 55 knots at full power in level flight, and a power-off stall speed of 24 knots or less.

facts.label: What you do not need
facts.value: No airworthiness certificate, no registration or markings, and no knowledge, age or experience requirement. No pilot certificate and no medical certificate.

facts.label: Daylight only
facts.value: Sunrise to sunset. Twilight flying, 30 minutes before sunrise and 30 minutes after sunset, needs an operating anticollision light visible for 3 statute miles and uncontrolled airspace only.

facts.label: Right of way
facts.value: See and avoid, and yield to all aircraft. Powered ultralights also yield to unpowered ultralights.

facts.label: Where you may not fly
facts.value: Over a congested area or an open air assembly of people. In Class A, B, C or D airspace, or inside the surface area of Class E airspace at an airport, only with prior ATC authorization.

facts.label: Weather minimums
facts.value: Set by airspace class in a table. Class G at or below 1,200 feet above the ground needs 1 statute mile and clear of clouds. You must always keep visual reference with the surface.

requirements.text: Single occupant. The vehicle is used, or intended to be used, for manned operation in the air by one person. A vehicle with a second seat does not qualify.
Recreation or sport only. Flying to do a job, such as patrolling, advertising or aerial spraying, is outside Part 103.
No airworthiness certificate. The vehicle holds no U.S. or foreign airworthiness certificate.
If unpowered, the vehicle weighs less than 155 pounds.

If powered, the empty weight is under 254 pounds, not counting floats and safety devices meant for deployment in a potentially catastrophic situation. The fuel capacity is 5 U.S. gallons or less. It cannot fly faster than 55 knots calibrated airspeed at full power in level flight. Its power-off stall speed is 24 knots calibrated airspeed or less.
Allow the FAA to inspect the vehicle on request, and furnish satisfactory evidence that it is subject only to Part 103.
Operations that need a deviation from Part 103 require a written waiver from the FAA.
Do not operate in a manner that creates a hazard to people or property, and do not allow an object to be dropped if that creates a hazard.

Fly only between sunrise and sunset, except in the twilight periods with an operating anticollision light visible for at least 3 statute miles and only in uncontrolled airspace. In Alaska the twilight period is civil twilight.
Maintain vigilance to see and avoid aircraft, yield the right of way to all aircraft, and never create a collision hazard. Powered ultralights yield to unpowered ultralights.
Do not operate over any congested area of a city, town or settlement, or over any open air assembly of persons.

Do not operate in Class A, B, C or D airspace, or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport, without prior authorization from the ATC facility that has jurisdiction.
Do not operate in prohibited or restricted areas without permission from the using or controlling agency.
Do not operate in areas designated by a NOTAM under 91.137, 91.138, 91.141, 91.143 or 91.145 unless authorized by ATC or by a Flight Standards Certificate of Waiver or Authorization for the event.
Fly only by visual reference with the surface.
Keep at least the flight visibility and cloud distance in the table in 103.23 for the airspace you are in.

There is no pilot certificate, medical certificate, age rule, knowledge test, aircraft registration or marking requirement under Part 103. State and local laws and the permission of landowners and airport managers still apply.

plan.focus: Learn what Part 103 is and prove your own vehicle meets 103.1. Then learn the operating rules. Read all of Part 103 twice, once at the start of the week and once at the end.
Learn the airspace classes and how to ask for ATC authorization. Buy or download a current sectional chart and trace the airspace around your flying field.
Study weather for slow aircraft, then how canopies and wings fly, then your engine and fuel. Write your personal weather limits at the end of the week.
Build your preflight checklist, rehearse emergencies out loud, and plan your training. Take the Part 103 practice test and review every question you miss.

after: Book lessons with a qualified instructor if you have not flown with one. Part 103 does not require training, and training is the best safety purchase you can make.
Weigh your vehicle on a calibrated scale and measure the fuel tank. Keep the records with the vehicle so you can show the FAA that it meets 103.1.
Write your preflight checklist and your personal weather limits, and keep both with the vehicle.
If your vehicle is over the 103.1 limits, or you want to carry a passenger, look at the sport pilot certificate path instead.
Take the Part 103 practice test again after a month. Use the Aha Trivia lessons for short reviews.

modules.title: What Part 103 is and the vehicle limits
modules.summary: What makes a vehicle an ultralight under 14 CFR 103.1, what Part 103 gives you and takes away, and why the pilot has to prove the vehicle qualifies.
objectives: State each vehicle limit in 103.1 for powered and unpowered ultralights.
Explain which weights count toward the 254 pound limit and which do not.
Explain why 55 knots, 24 knots and 5 gallons are tests of the vehicle, not rules for the pilot.
List what Part 103 does not require and what it still requires.
Say what happens when a vehicle fails any one limit.
Say whether the MOSAIC rule changed Part 103.

sections.heading: The vehicle and the flight both have to qualify
points: Part 103 is a short set of rules for a narrow kind of flying. A vehicle is an ultralight under Part 103 only if every item in 103.1 is true. The name on the brochure does not decide it. Words like ultralight, paramotor, trike or powered parachute are marketing until you check the numbers.

If any single item fails, Part 103 does not apply. The vehicle is then an aircraft and the full set of aircraft rules applies to it and to you. AC 103-7, the FAA circular on the ultralight vehicle, puts the burden on the operator. The maker or the kit builder is not the one who answers to the FAA. You answer for meeting 103.1 on every flight.

sections.heading: Four tests every ultralight must pass
points: The first test is one occupant. The vehicle is used, or intended to be used, for manned flight by a single person. AC 103-7 says that any provision for a second person disqualifies a vehicle, even when only one person is aboard. A bench seat that was sold as two-place does not qualify.

The second test is recreation or sport only. If you fly to do a task, you are outside Part 103. AC 103-7 gives examples: towing a banner, patrolling a fence line or power line, spraying crops, carrying parcels for hire, or advertising your services as a pilot. Winning a prize at a contest or writing a book about your flying does not count as flying for pay.

The third test is no airworthiness certificate. If the vehicle holds a U.S. or foreign airworthiness certificate, it cannot be flown under Part 103. AC 103-7 says the owner can turn the certificate in and then fly it as an ultralight if all other items are met.
The fourth test is the weight, fuel and speed limits below.

sections.heading: Limits for a powered ultralight
points: Empty weight must be under 254 pounds. Floats and safety devices meant for deployment in a potentially catastrophic situation are not counted. The ballistic parachute on many paramotors and trikes is the standard example. AC 103-7 says the FAA may exclude up to 24 pounds for a parachute system without weighing the parts separately, and that seat belts, roll cages, instruments and wheel brakes count as airframe weight.

Fuel capacity must be 5 U.S. gallons or less. This is the size of the tank, including fuel you cannot use. It is not how much you put in. AC 103-7 accepts a permanent standpipe or vent that limits a tank. It does not accept a fill-to line or any other limit that a pilot can ignore.

The vehicle must not be able to fly faster than 55 knots calibrated airspeed at full power in level flight. This is a performance limit of the vehicle. It is not a speed limit for the pilot. Flying slowly on purpose does not help a vehicle that can exceed 55 knots. AC 103-7 says a restriction counts only if the pilot cannot change it in flight.

The power-off stall speed must be 24 knots calibrated airspeed or less. AC 103-7 explains how to calculate it. For these calculations a 170 pound pilot and a full tank at 6 pounds per gallon are assumed.
For a rough feel, 55 knots is about 63 miles per hour and 24 knots is about 28 miles per hour.

sections.heading: Limit for an unpowered ultralight
points: An unpowered ultralight, such as a hang glider, a paraglider or a free balloon, must weigh less than 155 pounds. AC 103-7 says parachutes and personal operating equipment are not included in that weight. The other items in 103.1 still apply: one occupant, sport use only, and no airworthiness certificate.

sections.heading: What Part 103 does not require
points: Section 103.7 removes three big requirements. First, the vehicle and its parts do not need to meet airworthiness standards or have an airworthiness certificate. Second, the pilot has no aeronautical knowledge, age or experience requirement, and needs no airman certificate and no medical certificate. Third, the vehicle does not need to be registered or carry markings.

That is freedom from paperwork, not freedom from rules. The operating rules in Subpart B, the airspace rules, and state and local laws all still apply. A landowner or airport manager can still say no. The FAA can still inspect your vehicle under 103.3.

sections.heading: Proof and inspection
points: Section 103.3 says you must let the FAA inspect the vehicle on request, and you must give satisfactory evidence that it is subject only to Part 103. Keep that evidence with the vehicle. AC 103-7 lists good proof: a weight reading from a calibrated scale, a measurement of the fuel tank, and the maker's data for speed and stall speed.

AC 103-7 says an inspector can ask you to show compliance by measuring the fuel tank, weighing the vehicle and showing that any speed-limiting part is installed and cannot be bypassed. If you cannot prove it, the FAA treats the vehicle as an aircraft.

sections.heading: MOSAIC did not change Part 103
points: The FAA's MOSAIC rule, Modernization of Special Airworthiness Certification, was published in the Federal Register on July 24, 2025 and took effect October 22, 2025. It changed light-sport aircraft and sport pilot rules. It amended 14 CFR parts 1, 21, 22, 36, 43, 45, 61, 65, 91, 119 and 147. It did not amend Part 103.

The current text of 103.1 through 103.23 is unchanged. The last amendments shown in the eCFR notes are from 1991 (103.17 and 103.23) and 2001 (103.20). MOSAIC does matter if your vehicle is too heavy or too fast for Part 103, because the rules for the sport pilot path changed. Lesson 10 covers that.

Less than 254 pounds (floats and deployable safety devices not counted)
5 U.S. gallons or less

numbers.value: Not more than 55 knots calibrated airspeed
24 knots calibrated airspeed or less

traps: Thinking that any vehicle under 254 pounds qualifies. Weight is only one of the tests. Fuel capacity, top speed, stall speed, one seat and sport use also decide it.
Reading 5 gallons as how much fuel you may carry. The limit is the size of the tank. A fill-to line does not count.
Believing that flying slowly or throttling back keeps a fast machine legal. Section 103.1(e)(3) is about what the vehicle can do at full power.
Counting the ballistic parachute in the 254 pounds. Safety devices meant for a catastrophic situation are excluded. Seat belts, instruments and brakes are not.
Hearing no pilot certificate and thinking there are no rules. The operating rules and the airspace rules fully apply.
Trusting the manufacturer's label. The operator must be able to prove that the vehicle meets 103.1.

check.q: Which of these is NOT a requirement for a powered ultralight under 103.1?
choices: Fuel capacity of 5 U.S. gallons or less
A power-off stall speed of 24 knots or less
The pilot holds a sport pilot certificate
check.why: Part 103 requires no pilot certificate at all. The other three are limits in 103.1(e).

check.q: A paramotor has a ballistic parachute system. How does the parachute affect the 254 pound empty weight limit?
choices: It is not counted, because it is a safety device meant for deployment in a catastrophic situation
It counts only if it weighs more than 24 pounds
Only floats are excluded, never parachutes
check.why: Section 103.1(e)(1) excludes floats and safety devices intended for deployment in a potentially catastrophic situation.

check.q: A powered machine can reach 62 knots at full power in level flight, but the owner always flies it at 50 knots. May it be flown under Part 103?
choices: Yes, because the pilot never goes above 55 knots
No, because 103.1(e)(3) limits what the vehicle is capable of, not how the pilot flies it
Yes, if the owner paints a red line at 55 knots
check.why: The 55 knot limit is a performance limit of the vehicle. AC 103-7 says voluntary limits do not count.

check.q: Who has to show that the vehicle meets 103.1?
check.why: Section 103.3(b) says the pilot or operator must furnish satisfactory evidence that the vehicle is subject only to Part 103.

check.q: Did the MOSAIC rule of 2025 amend Part 103?
choices: Yes, it raised the weight limit
Yes, it added a pilot certificate
No, Part 103 was not amended by MOSAIC
Yes, it removed the 5 gallon limit
check.why: MOSAIC amended other parts, including 1, 21, 61 and 91, but not Part 103.

modules.title: Operating rules: daylight, crowds, right of way and hazards
modules.summary: The Subpart B rules you follow every flight: no hazards, daylight, see and avoid, no flying over crowds or towns, restricted areas, flight restrictions and visual reference.
objectives: Apply the daylight and twilight rule in 103.11 to a real flight.
State who yields to whom under 103.13.
Explain what 103.15 means for route planning and engine-out risk.
Explain how to handle prohibited, restricted and temporary flight restriction areas.
Explain the hazard rule and the dropped-object rule in 103.9.
Explain the rule on visual reference with the surface.

sections.heading: Do not create a hazard (103.9)
points: The first operating rule is the broadest. You may not operate in a way that creates a hazard to other people or property. You also may not allow an object to be dropped from the vehicle if that creates a hazard. The rule gives no list, so you judge it. Low passes over people, animals or buildings, flying close to another aircraft, and letting a tool, camera or water bottle fall are all risks.

AC 103-6 notes that noise is probably the most limiting factor for the sport. Angry neighbors lead to local rules. Fly high enough and far enough from houses and livestock that your engine does not cause trouble. A rule against hazards also covers hazards to you: a flight that cannot end in a safe landing is a hazard.

sections.heading: Sunrise to sunset, and the twilight exception (103.11)
points: You may fly only between sunrise and sunset. This is a daylight rule for the whole flight, not only the takeoff. Plan to be on the ground before sunset, with time to land, secure the wing and pack up.

There is one exception. During the 30 minutes before official sunrise and the 30 minutes after official sunset you may fly if two things are true. The vehicle has an operating anticollision light that can be seen for at least 3 statute miles. And every part of the flight is in uncontrolled airspace. In Alaska the exception uses the civil twilight period from the Air Almanac instead of 30 minutes.

Look up sunrise and sunset for your field on the day, from an official source such as the U.S. Naval Observatory. Light fades earlier in a valley or under tall trees. Gusts and thermals often calm near sunset, which tempts pilots to stay up late. Land with a margin.

sections.heading: See and avoid, and yield (103.13)
points: You must stay alert to see and avoid aircraft, and you must yield the right of way to all aircraft. You may not create a collision hazard. Powered ultralights must also yield to unpowered ultralights, such as paragliders and hang gliders.

You are slow, and other aircraft are usually much faster. The Powered Parachute Flying Handbook warns that fast aircraft can overtake a powered parachute quickly, so scanning matters in all airspace and most near airports without towers. AC 103-6 adds that wake turbulence from faster, heavier aircraft can be dangerous. Stay away from the paths of other aircraft and give them room.
Yielding is not a favor. It is the rule, and it also protects you. A collision between an ultralight and any other aircraft ends badly for the ultralight.

sections.heading: Congested areas and open air assemblies (103.15)
points: You may not operate over any congested area of a city, town or settlement, or over any open air assembly of persons. The rule gives no minimum altitude, so there is no height at which it becomes legal to fly over a town. Open air assemblies include ball games, fairs, outdoor concerts and crowded beaches.

Plan your route around towns, not over them. This rule matches good engine-out planning. If a two-stroke engine quits over rooftops, you have no place to land. AC 103-6 also reminds pilots that engine noise carries into a congested area even when the vehicle is not directly over it.

sections.heading: Prohibited areas, restricted areas and flight restrictions (103.19 and 103.20)
points: You may not fly in a prohibited or restricted area unless you have permission from the using or controlling agency. These areas are on the sectional chart. Restricted areas are often active only at certain times, so the controlling agency is the one to ask.

Section 103.20 covers areas that the FAA closes by Notice to Airmen (NOTAM). The rule names sections 91.137, 91.138, 91.141, 91.143 and 91.145. In plain words these cover disaster and hazard areas, national disaster areas in Hawaii, areas around the President and other protected parties, space flight operations, and aerial demonstrations and major sporting events. You may fly in such an area only if ATC authorizes it, or if a Flight Standards Certificate of Waiver or Authorization was issued for the event.
Check temporary flight restrictions before every flight. The FAA's TFR website shows current restrictions on a map. A fly-in, an air show or a stadium event can create one near your field.

sections.heading: Visual reference with the surface (103.21)
points: You may operate only with visual reference to the surface. That means you can see the ground. Flying above a cloud layer or fog, where you cannot see the ground, breaks this rule. Flying inside a cloud does too. The cloud and visibility minimums in 103.23 are a separate rule, covered in the weather lesson, and both apply at once.

sections.heading: Waivers, and rules outside Part 103
points: If you want to do something that Part 103 does not allow, you need a written waiver from the FAA under 103.5. A phone call to a friendly controller is not a waiver.

Part 91, the general operating rules for aircraft, does not apply to a vehicle governed by Part 103, according to 91.1(e). That is why Part 103 has its own visibility table and its own right-of-way rule. Other laws apply to you: state aviation laws, local noise and zoning rules, and the rights of landowners. AC 103-6 advises you to get permission from the landowner and to learn the terrain and obstacles before using a site.

traps: Treating the twilight exception as extra time for anyone. You need the light and uncontrolled airspace.
Landing at sunset instead of before it. The rule is about flying, so the whole flight must end before sunset unless the twilight exception applies.

Assuming a quiet field means no traffic. Fast aircraft can appear from behind you.
Skipping the TFR check because nothing was in the news. Events create restrictions on short notice.
Thinking visual reference to the surface is the same as the cloud clearance rule. They are two separate rules and both must be met.

check.why: Powered ultralights must yield to unpowered ultralights, and all ultralights yield to all aircraft.

modules.title: Airspace and ATC authorization
modules.summary: The airspace classes in plain words, which ones need ATC authorization under 103.17, how to ask for it, and how to stay out of airspace you cannot enter.
objectives: Describe Classes A, B, C, D, E and G in plain words.
Name the airspace where 103.17 requires prior ATC authorization.
Explain why most low-level flying near a small field needs no authorization.
Describe how to ask a facility for authorization and what to expect.
Plan a route around airspace you cannot enter.
Explain how special use airspace and military routes affect an ultralight.

sections.heading: Why airspace is your job
points: Nobody tests an ultralight pilot on airspace, but the airspace rules apply to you in full. The airspace does not know you are an ultralight. If you enter a Class D area without authorization, you have broken 103.17, and you may also be a collision risk to airliners and other traffic that expect only communicating aircraft.

Part 91 does not apply to vehicles under Part 103 (91.1(e)). That means Part 91 equipment and communication rules for airspace do not apply to you directly. Section 103.17 and the controlling facility do the work instead, and ATC can attach conditions to an authorization.

sections.heading: The classes in plain words
points: Class A is from 18,000 feet MSL up to flight level 600. You will not be there. Class B surrounds the busiest airports. It goes from the surface up to about 10,000 feet MSL in layers that look like an upside-down wedding cake. Class C surrounds airports with a tower and radar approach control. It usually has a 5 nautical mile core up to 4,000 feet above the airport and a 10 nautical mile shelf that starts no lower than 1,200 feet.

Class D surrounds airports with a control tower. It goes from the surface to about 2,500 feet above the airport. Some Class D areas are part-time. When the tower closes, the area changes to a Class E surface area or to Class G. The Chart Supplement entry for the airport says which, with wording such as other times Class E or other times Class G.

Class E is controlled airspace that is not A, B, C or D. It has several forms. A Class E surface area is designated for an airport with no tower or with a closed tower. Other Class E airspace starts at 700 feet above the ground, or at 1,200 feet above the ground, or higher. Class G is uncontrolled airspace, the space under the Class E floor and anywhere with no controlled airspace.

Altitudes are in feet above mean sea level (MSL) on charts, except where they say above ground level (AGL). The floor of Class E at 700 or 1,200 feet is AGL, which is why the chart shows it by a band and not by a number.

sections.heading: Where 103.17 requires authorization
points: Section 103.17 says you may not operate within Class A, B, C or D airspace, or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport, unless you have prior authorization from the ATC facility that has jurisdiction.

Read what is not on that list. Class E that begins at 700 or 1,200 feet above the ground and Class G are not covered. A flight from a farm field in Class G needs no authorization under 103.17, even if it is below a large Class E shelf. You still have to meet the visibility and cloud rules in 103.23, and every other rule.

Class E extensions are drawn on the chart as dashed lines that extend from a surface area. The AIM says arrival extensions to a Class E surface area become part of the surface area. When your route crosses one, treat it as part of the surface area and ask the facility if you are not sure.

sections.heading: How to get authorization
points: You need authorization before you enter, not as you enter. Find the facility that has jurisdiction. For a Class D airport that is usually the tower. For Class B, Class C and many Class E surface areas it is usually an approach control. If you are not sure, AC 103-6 says to ask your nearest Flight Service or tower, which can point you to the right facility.

AC 103-6 was written in 1983, but its advice still reads well. It says to ask by letter, phone or in person at the facility, because requests on a busy radio frequency are normally not accepted. Ask the facility how it prefers to receive requests. A call to the tower or approach control during a quiet time is the usual way.

Be ready with who you are, a phone number, the type of vehicle, its speed, the place, the altitude, the date and time, and how long you want to stay. Say whether you carry a radio and a light. Expect conditions such as a route, an altitude, a time window or a landing area. AC 103-6 says controllers have been told to authorize ultralights only if they can be kept clear of normal aircraft, so expect to be separated from other traffic and to handle your own spacing.

ATC may say no. AC 103-6 lists the reasons: the kind of flight, the effect on other traffic, controller workload and equipment. A denial is not personal. Write down the controller's name, the time and any conditions, and keep the note with you. If you do not have a clear yes, stay out.

sections.heading: Staying out of airspace you cannot enter
points: The Powered Parachute Flying Handbook tells pilots to review the airspace in preflight planning and to plan a course around airspace they cannot enter. That costs extra time and fuel, so include both in the plan.

Pilotage means navigating by landmarks. The handbook calls it the best way to avoid airspace you are not allowed to enter. It also calls GPS a popular tool but warns that the GPS airspace data may not match the sectional chart. If they differ, the handbook says the sectional chart is the correct information. Leave a buffer when you avoid airspace with GPS, and keep your batteries fresh and your database current. Never depend on GPS alone.

sections.heading: Other airspace you must know
points: Prohibited areas and restricted areas need permission under 103.19. Military operations areas (MOAs), alert areas and warning areas are not banned to you, but they can hold fast military aircraft or other unusual activity. Check the chart and call Flight Service for the status of any you plan to fly near. The AIM explains each type in chapter 3.

Military training routes appear on sectional charts as gray lines with VR or IR numbers. AC 103-6 says that most are below 10,000 feet MSL and used at speeds above 250 knots. You are not banned from them, but you are slow and hard to see, so call for the route status before you fly near one.

Parachute jump areas, glider fields and flight parks hold other slow traffic. AIM 3-5 covers parachute jump aircraft operations. Temporary flight restrictions are covered in the operating rules lesson.

sections.heading: Airports without a tower
points: At a field with no tower you have no controller to guide you. The handbook says powered parachutes should stay out of the flow of fixed-wing traffic and set up away from the runway centerline. Do not tie up an active runway while you lay out a wing. Walk to a safe area or ask the airport manager where to set up.

Look at the windsock, the other aircraft and the traffic pattern before you decide where to launch or land. Faster aircraft may enter the pattern from any side. Use a radio on the field's common frequency if you have one and know how. Do not rely on a radio call to protect you. Your eyes do that.

traps: Thinking all controlled airspace needs authorization. Class E that starts at 700 or 1,200 feet above the ground is not on the 103.17 list.
Assuming a closed tower means free access. A part-time Class D becomes a Class E surface area or Class G. Only Class G is free of 103.17.
Trusting a GPS airspace shape over the sectional chart. The handbook says to treat the chart as correct.
Calling the tower on the radio when you are one minute from the boundary. Ask before you fly, and stay out until you have an answer.
Assuming Part 91 radio and transponder rules protect you. They do not apply to you, so you have to avoid traffic yourself.

modules.title: Reading a sectional chart
modules.summary: How to read the VFR sectional chart: scale, edition dates, airspace lines and bands, airports, obstacles and special use areas, and how to plan a low, slow flight with it.
objectives: Say the scale of a sectional chart and how to check that your chart is current.
Identify Class B, C, D and E airspace lines and the 700 and 1,200 foot Class E bands.
Read altitudes on the chart and tell MSL from AGL.
Find towered and non-towered airports, obstacles and special use airspace.
Use the Chart Supplement with the chart.
Plan a local flight with the chart and use GPS only as a backup.

sections.heading: What a sectional is
points: A sectional chart is the VFR map pilots use to find airspace, airports, towers, terrain and obstacles. Its scale is 1:500,000. One inch on the chart equals 6.86 nautical miles, which is about 8 statute miles. That is a lot of ground on a small sheet, so a short local flight may sit under a thumbnail.

The Powered Parachute Flying Handbook calls the current sectional the primary official tool to find the airspace you fly in or want to avoid. Terminal Area Charts show Class B areas at a larger scale of 1:250,000, which helps near big airports.

sections.heading: Keep your chart current
points: A chart has an edition and an effective date printed on it. Airspace changes, towers appear and new obstacles go up. A chart that is a year old can send you into airspace that did not exist when it was printed. The PHAK says sectionals are reissued about twice a year. The FAA publishes changed charts in 56-day sets. Look at the date on the chart you hold, and compare it with the FAA's chart page.
The chart legend explains every symbol. Read it once, slowly, before you rely on the chart. The FAA also publishes a Chart User's Guide with the symbols.

sections.heading: Airspace on the chart
points: Controlled airspace is drawn with color. Class B is a solid blue line. Class C is a solid magenta line. Class D is a dashed blue line. A dashed magenta line marks a Class E surface area. Check these on the legend of your own chart, because the legend is the authority.

Class E that starts above the ground is shown with a faded band. A magenta band means Class E begins at 700 feet above the ground. A blue band means it begins at 1,200 feet above the ground. If no band is drawn, the Class E floor is higher, or the airspace is Class G. Class E with the floor of 700 feet matters, because it can cover a large area around a small airport.

Numbers near airspace boundaries are altitudes in hundreds of feet MSL. A number like 25 means 2,500 feet MSL. On layered airspace like Class B, the top number is the ceiling and the bottom number is the floor. Learn the format from the legend.
Only some of this airspace blocks you. Class B, Class C, Class D and Class E surface areas need 103.17 authorization. A faded band by itself does not.

sections.heading: Airports, towers and frequencies
points: Airports with control towers are shown in blue and all other airports in magenta. The airport symbol has the name, the field elevation in feet MSL, the longest runway in hundreds of feet, and the tower or common frequency. The AC 103-6 circular makes the same point: a blue airport symbol tells you a control tower is there.

The chart does not hold everything. The Chart Supplement gives runway details, tower hours, frequencies, phone numbers and airspace status for each airport. Use it to see whether a tower is part-time. The Chart Supplement is revised every 56 days.

sections.heading: Obstacles, hazards and special use airspace
points: Towers and other tall obstacles are shown with a symbol and two numbers. One is the top in feet MSL. The other, in parentheses, is the height above the ground. Low-level pilots must watch for tall structures, guy wires and power lines. Many wires and small towers are not on the chart, so look out for them and scout your field on the ground.

Restricted and prohibited areas, military operations areas, warning areas and alert areas are drawn with hatched borders and names such as R-2301 or P-56. The legend tells you the type and the color. The chart margin or a side panel lists the altitudes, the times and the controlling agency. Military training routes are gray lines with VR or IR numbers.

sections.heading: Planning a local flight
points: Start by marking the airspace near your field. Draw a line around anything that needs authorization. Decide how far you will stay from it. Use roads, rivers, towers and other landmarks that you can see from a low, slow aircraft. This is pilotage, and the handbook calls it the best way to avoid airspace.

Measure distances on the chart, then work out the time. At 30 miles per hour you cover 1 mile in 2 minutes. Leave extra time and fuel to go around airspace. Mark the possible landing fields along the route. Keep a note of the tower and common frequencies and the phone numbers of the facilities you may need.

sections.heading: GPS and phone charts
points: Many pilots carry GPS or phone charts. They are useful. They are not the official chart, and the handbook warns that the airspace data in a GPS may not exactly match the sectional. If you use one, check that its database is current, its battery is fresh, and you have a buffer from airspace edges. Always carry a paper or downloaded copy of the current sectional as well.

modules.title: Weather for low and slow flying
modules.summary: The visibility and cloud rules in 103.23, why wind is the main limit for light aircraft, how to find and read weather, and how to set personal limits.
objectives: Use the 103.23 table to find the visibility and cloud clearance for any airspace.
Explain why steady, light wind is the target and why gusts and shear are the danger.
Read the wind and visibility parts of a METAR.
Explain thermals, mechanical turbulence and density altitude in simple terms.
Name the sources for a weather briefing and for wind at your field.
Write personal weather limits that are tighter than the legal minimums.

sections.heading: The legal minimums (103.23)
points: Section 103.23 gives a table of minimum flight visibility and distance from clouds. It looks much like the Part 91 VFR table, but it is its own rule, because Part 91 does not apply to vehicles under Part 103. Read this table and do not rely on memory of the Part 91 one. In Class G at 1,200 feet or less above the ground, you need 1 statute mile of visibility and must stay clear of clouds. In Class G above 1,200 feet above the ground and below 10,000 feet MSL, you need 1 statute mile and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds. At or above 10,000 feet MSL in Class G you need 5 statute miles and 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontally.

In Class E below 10,000 feet MSL, you need 3 statute miles and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally. At or above 10,000 feet MSL in Class E, it is 5 statute miles and 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontally. In Class B you need 3 statute miles and clear of clouds. In Class C and D you need 3 statute miles and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally. Class A is listed as not applicable.

Remember that all of these are minimums for the law. You must also keep visual reference with the surface (103.21), and ATC authorization is still needed for Class A, B, C, D and Class E surface areas. Good judgment for a slow, light aircraft puts your own limits far above these.

sections.heading: Wind is the main limit
points: Heavy, fast aircraft cut through wind. A canopy or a light airframe gets pushed around. The handbook says powered parachutes fly best in calm air, that winds under 10 miles per hour are ideal, and that steady wind is better than gusty wind. Five miles per hour with no gusts is better than 1 mile per hour gusting to 5. Follow the maker's limits for your wing and aircraft, and remember that they may be lower than your skill allows.

AC 103-6 suggests it may be wise not to fly ultralights in winds above 15 miles per hour, and that even then there are times when 15 is too much. It also notes that wind often drops near the ground and that sudden changes at low altitude can cause a stall. USPPA lists a maximum wind of 8 miles per hour, including gusts, for its student-level PPG 1 pilots. These are guides from different sources. Your limits should be set for your skill and your aircraft, and written down.

Crosswind takeoffs are dangerous in a powered parachute and should be avoided. The wing weathervanes into the wind, so you want the cart pointed into the wind as you lay out. If the field only allows a crosswind takeoff, cancel or move.

sections.heading: Gusts, shear and the danger zone near the ground
points: AC 103-6 says that the most critical altitudes for sudden changes of wind are between 30 and 75 feet above the ground. A gust can lift a light aircraft and then drop away, leaving the pilot in a stall close to the ground. A wind that is strong aloft and calm at the surface can drop your airspeed as you descend. Keep extra airspeed near the ground in gusty conditions, if your aircraft allows it.

Nearby hills, trees and buildings make the wind chaotic. The handbook says turbulence from an upwind obstacle can reach from the surface to about 10 times the height of the obstacle, and says to avoid flying in it. For a 50 foot line of trees, that is up to about 500 feet of rough air.

sections.heading: Thermals and time of day
points: The sun heats the ground unevenly. Hot ground makes rising columns of air called thermals, with sinking air between them. Plowed fields, parking lots and rock heat quickly. Water, forest and wet fields stay cooler. A midday flight over mixed ground can be bumpy. Morning and evening air is usually smoother, but you must still be inside the daylight rule.

Distant storms matter too. A storm's downdraft can spread out along the ground as a gust front and reach you before the cloud does. If you see towering clouds or a dark base in the distance, do not launch. If you are flying, land.

sections.heading: Density altitude and engines
points: Hot, humid air at a high field is thin. The wing makes less lift and the propeller makes less thrust. The handbook says that a powered parachute that cleared an obstacle at 8 a.m. may not clear it at 1 p.m., when it is hotter. Expect a longer takeoff roll and a weaker climb on hot days and at higher fields.

Fog and haze matter as well. The handbook says to watch for low visibility when the air temperature and dew point are within three or four degrees of each other, because fog is more likely when they are close.

sections.heading: Where to get weather
points: Get a full briefing before you go. The handbook lists the National Weather Service and 1-800-WX-BRIEF. The Flight Service website 1800wxbrief.com gives a briefing online. The Aviation Weather Center website aviationweather.gov shows METARs, TAFs, pilot reports and graphical forecasts. The NWS site gives hourly wind and gust forecasts for a point on the map, which is often the most useful forecast for a field with no airport.

A METAR is a coded airport report. Example: KXYZ 251453Z 18008G15KT 10SM FEW040 24/18 A2992. It reads: station KXYZ, the 25th day at 1453 UTC, wind from 180 degrees at 8 knots gusting to 15, visibility 10 statute miles, few clouds at 4,000 feet, temperature 24 and dew point 18 degrees Celsius, altimeter 29.92. Multiply knots by 1.15 to get miles per hour: 8 knots is about 9 mph and 15 knots is about 17 mph.

An airport report is not your field. The nearest reporting station may be many miles away. Look at your own windsock or streamers. AC 103-6 suggests several streamers around a site and also tells how a glassy patch on a lake shows wind direction, with the glass reaching further out when the wind is lighter.

sections.heading: Personal minimums
points: The handbook tells pilots to build their own set of personal minimums that grow with experience, and that depend on how recently you flew the aircraft. Write yours down before you need them. Include steady wind, gust spread, visibility, how far a storm must be, and how long since your last flight. Decide the numbers on the ground, in calm conditions. Do not decide at the field when you want to fly.

Example only, not a rule: no flight if gusts are more than a few miles per hour above the steady wind, or if the wind is above the lowest of the maker's limit and your own. Your numbers should come from your instructor and your maker.

modules.title: How wings and canopies fly
modules.summary: Lift, drag, angle of attack and stalls for flexible wings. How a ram-air canopy holds its shape, how a powered parachute and a weight-shift trike are controlled, and what makes each one dangerous.
objectives: Name the four forces and say how they balance in steady flight.
Explain how a ram-air canopy holds its shape and why airflow matters.
Explain pendulum stability and why throttle does not change airspeed in a powered parachute.
Explain angle of attack and list what can cause a stall.
Explain how a weight-shift trike is controlled and what a whip stall is.
Describe how banking raises load and speed.

sections.heading: The four forces
points: Four forces act on every aircraft. Lift holds it up. Weight pulls it down. Thrust pushes it forward. Drag pulls it back. In steady, level flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag. Lift grows with the square of the airspeed, so doubling the speed gives four times the lift. The same square rule applies to parasite drag. Lift and drag also depend on air density, wing area and the angle of attack.

Drag has two kinds. Induced drag comes from making lift. Parasite drag comes from pushing every other part through the air: lines, cart, pilot, engine and wheels. A powered parachute has a lot of parasite drag. It flies slowly, so the maker does not fair these parts.

sections.heading: How a ram-air canopy works
points: A ram-air canopy is made of cells. Air enters openings at the leading edge and pressurizes each cell. Small cross-ports in the ribs keep the pressure the same through the wing. The pressure comes from the wind that hits the openings, so the wing keeps its airfoil shape only while air flows in. That is why takeoff starts with kiting: you move forward until the wing fills and rises.

The shape stays about the same in flight, but the pilot changes it. Pulling down on the trailing edge on one side adds drag and turns the wing. Pulling both sides down is a flare. The handbook compares it to lowering flaps on an airplane. Higher speeds and heavier loads put more pressure in the wing and raise control forces.

sections.heading: Pendulum stability and what the throttle does
points: In a powered parachute, the cart hangs well below the wing, like a pendulum. Gravity keeps the cart under the wing, and that makes the aircraft stable. When something disturbs it, the cart swings back under the wing.

The wing sets its own speed. The trim angle is fixed at the factory, so airspeed is set mostly by the weight and the wing design. Adding throttle makes the aircraft climb. Reducing it makes the aircraft descend. Airspeed changes very little. The handbook gives the working rule that a powered parachute flies at a nearly constant speed and angle of attack as the throttle changes.

Because the cart swings, quick throttle changes make it swing forward and back, which is called porpoising. A big, sudden throttle move can set up pitch oscillations. Move the throttle smoothly. The handbook lists porpoising from rapid throttle movement as a usual cause of landing accidents.

sections.heading: Angle of attack and stalls
points: Angle of attack is the angle between the wing and the oncoming air. A wing stalls when this angle gets too big, at any speed, weight or attitude. A powered parachute wing is built to fly in a narrow range of angle of attack. It is stall resistant when flown within the limits in the pilot's operating handbook, and it can collapse if the angle gets too low.

The handbook lists what can push a canopy toward a stall. A large increase in wing drag, such as a full flare, raises the angle. A sudden full-throttle input loads the wing as the cart swings. A fast throttle chop during a steep climb turns a high pitch into a high angle of attack. A strong gust does the same. The handbook says: do not go to full throttle while holding a full flare. Use full flare only for the landing.

sections.heading: Weight-shift trikes
points: A trike is a flexible hang glider wing with a powered, three-wheel carriage hanging beneath it. The pilot holds a control bar. Pushing the bar out raises the angle of attack and slows the aircraft. Pulling the bar in lowers the angle of attack and speeds it up. Moving the bar sideways shifts weight under the wing and banks the aircraft. Throttle adds power.

The WSC handbook calls out a danger special to this design: the whip stall. In a high nose attitude or in strong turbulence, the wingtips can stall. The weight is far forward and most wing area is behind it, so the nose drops hard. A mild case recovers. A severe case can tuck and tumble, and the handbook says a tumble has no recovery and brings structural failure. The cure is prevention: fly inside the maker's pitch and speed limits and stay out of strong turbulence. If the nose rotates down, push the bar out, level the wings and add full power, which creates a nose-up moment.

sections.heading: Paramotors and fixed-wing ultralights
points: A paramotor works like a powered parachute with the pilot's harness in place of the cart. The same ideas apply: pendulum stability, a wing that needs airflow to stay open, and propeller torque. The pilot's body weight also swings under the wing. Get the details of your wing and harness from your school.

Propeller torque is another idea from the powered parachute book. A clockwise-turning propeller tries to turn the cart the other way, and makers compensate with different riser lengths, a tilted attach bar or a different frame. This shows why you should never change an aircraft's risers or attachment without the maker's approval.

A conventional single-seat ultralight airplane follows the basics in the PHAK: three-axis control, angle of attack stalls, and stall speed that rises in a turn. A 60 degree bank doubles the load and raises the stall speed by about 41 percent.

sections.heading: Turns, load and speed
points: In a banked turn, the wing must carry more than the aircraft's weight, so the load goes up. The handbook gives an example with an 800 pound powered parachute in a 45 degree bank. The load is 1.4 times the weight, which is like adding 320 pounds. To make that extra lift the wing needs more speed or more angle of attack. In the example, if all the extra lift came from speed, the speed would rise about 5 mph.

A powered parachute has no ailerons, so it does not roll the way an airplane does. In a steep turn the cart swings out to the outside of the turn. Steep turns near the ground are risky for that reason. Keep turns shallow and smooth.

modules.title: Engines and fuel, with two-stroke basics
modules.summary: How a two-stroke engine works, how to mix fuel and oil, why warm-up matters, how carburetor ice forms, and how to handle fuel, fire and propeller risks.
objectives: Describe the two-stroke cycle in plain words.
Mix fuel and two-stroke oil safely at the right ratio.
Explain why a two-stroke engine needs warm-up before power.
Explain when and why carburetor ice forms.
Describe fuel handling, storage and static control.
Describe the propeller and starting dangers of a pusher engine.

sections.heading: How a two-stroke works
points: A two-stroke engine makes power on every turn of the crankshaft. When the piston moves up, it makes a vacuum in the crankcase. That draws a mix of fuel, air and oil in through the carburetor. When the piston moves down, it squeezes the mix in the crankcase and pushes it up into the cylinder through ports. Then the piston rises again, squeezes the mix, and a spark ignites it. Exhaust leaves through the exhaust port as new mix comes in.

Most two-stroke engines have no oil sump. The oil that lubricates the crankshaft, bearings and cylinder walls arrives with the fuel. If the oil is missing or wrong, the engine wears or seizes within minutes. This is why fuel and oil are the most important part of two-stroke care.

The handbook notes that powered parachute two-stroke engines grew out of snowmobile and watercraft engines. The handbook says powered parachute engines use a gearbox, so the propeller turns slower than the engine.

sections.heading: Mixing fuel and oil
points: Some engines have an oil injection pump that adds oil by itself. For those, the preflight check is to see that the oil tank is filled with the right oil. Other engines need pre-mixed fuel. The handbook says a mix ratio of 50 to 1 is usual for engines like this, but you must follow your engine maker's number. At 50 to 1, one U.S. gallon of fuel needs about 2.6 fluid ounces of oil, because a gallon is 128 fluid ounces and 128 divided by 50 is 2.56.

To mix: use a clean approved container. Pour in a little gasoline, add a measured amount of two-stroke oil, and shake so the oil thins. Add gasoline up to the right ratio. Cap the container and shake again. Do not pour oil into a tank full of fuel and hope it mixes. Mark every can with its contents. Pre-mixed fuel in an unmarked can can be mistaken for plain gasoline, and plain gasoline in a pre-mix engine will destroy it.
The handbook warns that pre-mixed fuel left in a plastic jug can lose gasoline by evaporation and leave a richer oil mix. Use fresh fuel when you can. Mix outdoors, not in a closed room.

sections.heading: Warm-up, and why
points: A two-stroke engine must warm up before you ask for power. Metals expand at different rates as they heat. Aluminum pistons and cylinders grow faster than steel parts, so clearances change as the engine warms. Applying power to a cold engine can seize a piston.

Follow your maker's warm-up routine. Watch the temperature gauges and learn the minimum, normal and maximum values. Check both ignitions if you have two, one at a time, and look for a small drop in RPM. The handbook says do not fly if the temperature readings are not normal. After a quick refuel, the lower end of the engine stays warm, so a short restart needs less time, but the cylinders still need to reach normal gauge readings.

sections.heading: Carburetor ice
points: A carburetor cools the air when the fuel vaporizes and when the air speeds up in the venturi. That can drop the temperature by 60 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit. If the air is moist, ice forms inside the carburetor, usually near the throat. The ice chokes the flow and the engine loses power, and it can stop.

The handbook says carburetor ice is most likely below 70 degrees Fahrenheit with humidity above 80 percent. It also says it can form at air temperatures as high as 100 degrees Fahrenheit with humidity as low as 50 percent. Find out whether your engine has any carburetor heat. If it does not, your protection is to avoid cool, damp conditions where ice is likely and to stay within reach of a landing area.

sections.heading: Fuel quality and storage
points: Clean fuel matters. The handbook says contamination often comes from fuel system dirt not cleared at preflight, fuel from small tanks or drums that was not filtered, partly filled tanks in storage and poor maintenance. Rust is common in metal containers. Fill metal tanks full after the last flight of the day so moist air cannot condense inside. Use a funnel that filters water when you fill from cans, and do not trust a damp or worn chamois to do the job.

Gasoline that sits for weeks goes bad and loses octane. Use fresh fuel. Use the fuel type and octane that your engine maker names. The handbook says most powered parachute engine makers recommend premium automotive fuel and that 100LL aviation gasoline is usually acceptable on a limited basis. Follow your maker, not a rule of thumb.

sections.heading: Refueling safely
points: Never mix fuel and oil in an enclosed area. The fumes can explode. Refuel outdoors. Never smoke when refueling. Be careful when you refuel right after landing, because spilled fuel on a hot exhaust can ignite. Use approved containers with their contents marked on the outside.

Static electricity can ignite fuel vapor. Plastic containers can build a charge, and fuel flowing through a hose, nozzle or chamois adds more. The handbook says to ground the aircraft before the cap comes off, to ground the nozzle or can to the aircraft, and to set plastic cans on the ground before filling. It also says not to use cell phones while refueling.

sections.heading: Pusher propellers and starting
points: A powered parachute, paramotor or trike engine usually pushes from behind. Suspension lines, wing material, loose clothing and bystanders are all near the propeller. Keep lines out of the prop arc. Do not start with the back of the cart pointed at people, a hangar or parked cars. Look around, call clear prop, and wait for an answer.

Keep one hand on the throttle and one on the ignition when you start, so you can shut down at once if the engine races. Do not hold the starter for more than 30 seconds without a cool-down of at least 30 seconds to a minute. If your engine has an oil pressure gauge and the pressure does not come up, shut down. After start, keep the RPM low until the engine runs smoothly.

sections.heading: Fuel planning with a small tank
points: Your tank cannot be larger than 5 gallons, so your range is limited by your fuel burn. Learn your real burn rate by timing refuels, not from a brochure. Part 103 sets no fuel reserve and Part 91 reserve rules do not apply, so set your own and write it down. The 30 minutes of reserve that Part 91 sets for airplanes in daytime VFR is a common starting point.

Check fuel visually before each flight. The handbook says to confirm the gauge reading by looking at the tank, because ramp slope and tank shape can fool a gauge. Land with the reserve you chose. Land early if the engine temperature, noise or vibration change.

modules.title: Preflight and the checklist habit
modules.summary: Why a written checklist matters when nobody requires one, how to walk around a powered parachute, paramotor or trike, and how to decide to fly or not to fly.
objectives: Explain why you are the only inspector for an ultralight.
List the five tasks in a powered parachute walk-around.
Check fuel, oil, propeller, exhaust, lines and wing in a fixed order.
Run an engine start, warm-up and run-up safely.
Decide when to abort and re-layout instead of taking off.
Build and keep a written checklist for your own aircraft.

sections.heading: You are the inspector
points: Part 103 sets no airworthiness standards and requires no inspection. Section 103.7(a) says the vehicle does not need an airworthiness certificate. No mechanic signs it off, and no one checks it before you fly. AC 103-7 says there is no assurance that a particular ultralight has consistent performance, controllability, structure or maintenance. It says safety depends on good preflight, flying within the maker's envelope, safe weather and safety devices for emergencies.

The handbook tells pilots to use a written checklist, because a checklist aids the memory and makes sure critical items are not missed. The same handbook estimates that about 85 percent of powered parachute accidents happen on takeoff, 10 percent on landing and 5 percent in flight, and that most come from complacency. A machine that is easy to fly invites the habit of skipping the check.

sections.heading: Before you leave home
points: Gather the facts for the day. Check the weather and the winds at your field. Check temporary flight restrictions. Look up sunrise and sunset and plan to land well before sunset. Look at the sectional chart for airspace near your field. Make sure you have permission from the landowner or airport manager.

Take your proof that the vehicle meets 103.1: weight record, tank size and the maker's speed and stall data. Tell someone where you will fly and when you expect to land. The handbook suggests filing a flight plan with Flight Service for cross-country flights and closing it afterward. Plan to carry a phone and, if you can, a radio.

sections.heading: The walk-around in a fixed order
points: The handbook breaks a powered parachute preflight into five tasks: cart inspection, powerplant inspection, equipment check, engine warm-up and check, and wing and suspension line inspection. Use the maker's checklist for your exact model, and do the steps in the same order every time. A trike or a paramotor has the same stages: frame and harness, engine, equipment, engine run, then wing and lines.

Start with the first look. Walk around the aircraft and look for damage from transport, low tires, bent tubes, leaking fuel or oil, and loose or missing hardware. Remove tie-downs and chocks. The handbook says not to over-handle the aircraft, but to shake the cart gently to find loose parts.

sections.heading: Airframe, controls and cables
points: Check the nosewheel and axle, tire pressure and condition, steering bar connections and brakes. Look at seats, rails and seat belts for wear or cracks. Move the throttle through its full range and feel for binding. Check cables for kinks, frays and broken strands, and check the ends for bolt security. Cords showing in a tire or cracked sidewalls make the tire unairworthy.
Set the ignition and battery switches off at the start. Turn them on later to test the parts they power. Check the strobe or anticollision light if you have one, since you may need it in twilight.

sections.heading: Fuel, oil and engine
points: Look in the tank to see the fuel level, and compare it with the gauge. Make sure the fuel type is right. Check the caps and the vent, and the inline filter for dirt or water. Check the oil level, and for an injected two-stroke check that the oil tank is vented. If you use pre-mix, confirm the mix ratio.

Look at the propeller for nicks, cracks, pitting and loose tape. Check that the hub bolts are secure. Because the engine is a pusher, look for loose items that could blow into the prop. Check carburetors, the air filter, rubber manifolds, spark plug caps, the gearbox for leaking seals and play, the exhaust for white stains or cracks and loose springs, and radiator fluid on a liquid-cooled engine.

sections.heading: Wing and lines
points: Check the wind direction first and point the cart into the wind before you lay out the wing. Pull the bag off without twisting it. Keep the marked side of the bag always facing the same way, so you can tell if the lines have twisted. Lay the wing out behind the cart and look at the fabric for tears, loose stitching and wear. Check the lines for knots, tangles, damage and twists. Check that the lines run straight, that no line is under a wheel or around a part of the frame, and that the line crossing in the center sits behind the middle of the propeller.

The wing must be centered and its cells must open as it comes up. If the wing is not centered or the cells have not opened, the handbook says do not add power to force it. Slow down or shut down, point the cart into the wind and build the wing again.

sections.heading: Start, warm-up and run-up
points: Do not point the back of the cart at people, a hangar door or parked cars. Look around, turn on the anticollision light if you have one, shout clear prop, and wait for an answer. Keep one hand on the throttle and one on the ignition. Keep the RPM low after start. Watch oil pressure if your engine has a gauge. Warm up as your maker says.

During the run-up, watch the temperature gauges and compare them to the limits. Check each ignition in turn and look for a small RPM drop, then back to both. Check that full RPM is reached. Do not fly if a reading is not normal. Figure out the problem on the ground.

sections.heading: The decision to go
points: A takeoff you abort costs a few minutes. A takeoff you continue with a wall in the wing, a line caught on something, or a high engine temperature can cost much more. The handbook says to abort and lay the wing out again rather than try to fix a bad wing with throttle.

Keep a short written checklist for your own aircraft, and keep it with the aircraft. Read it, do not recite it from memory. Add every item that has ever caught you out. If you are rushed or interrupted, start the checklist again from the top.

Reading the fuel gauge and not looking in the tank.
Doing the wing check in a hurry or from the wrong side. Twisted lines are easy to miss.
Adding power to fix a wing that is not centered or has closed cells. Shut down and build it again.
Skipping the run-up because the engine started easily.

modules.title: Emergencies and off-field landings
modules.summary: What to do when the engine quits, when the wing or lines go wrong on the ground, when there is fire, or when water is ahead. How to pick a landing field and survive afterward.
objectives: Explain why you should always have a place to land.
Describe the right response to engine failure on climb-out and in cruise.
Choose an off-field landing area and landing direction.
Describe flare timing for a power-off landing in a powered parachute.
Describe the response to fire, rollover, a wing wall and a lock-out.
Describe the main steps for a water landing and for a trike tumble.

sections.heading: Always have a place to land
points: The handbook gives one rule that prevents most engine-failure accidents: never fly over something you cannot land on, taking account of your altitude and glide. If you follow that rule, an engine failure is not an accident. You glide away from obstacles and toward the safest field.

This rule makes you choose routes that follow open farmland and avoid dense woods, water, towns and highways. It also means that altitude is not only for safety from the ground. Altitude gives you time and choices. Plan your route and your altitude together.

sections.heading: Engine failure after takeoff
points: You have only a few seconds. The handbook says to decide in advance what you will do. When the engine fails shortly after takeoff and you are low, it is usually unwise to turn back to the field. Set a glide attitude and land straight ahead or slightly to either side of the takeoff path.

In a powered parachute on initial climb, the cart sits at a high pitch angle, far in front of the wing. When the engine fails, the cart swings back under the wing and the wing can surge forward and cause a brief, dangerous dive. If the engine fails close to the ground and the wing surges ahead, flare at once to slow the surge. Release the flare gradually as the wing returns overhead.

In a weight-shift trike, the first job is to keep control. At climb pitch with no power the wing is near a stall. The WSC handbook says to lower the pitch right away by pulling the control bar to the chest, and then glide toward a landing area, preferably straight ahead. It also suggests keeping a low pitch angle and a bit more speed through about the first 200 feet as a precaution.

sections.heading: Engine failure in flight, and choosing the field
points: If the engine quits, keep flying the aircraft. Glide away from obstacles and toward the best field. The safest field might be in the middle of a flight park if you have plenty of altitude, or straight ahead if you are below about 100 feet.

Look for size, a smooth surface, no wires or fences, little slope and no people, animals or crops you could damage. The handbook says safe terrain is the first priority, and wind direction is second. Land into the wind if you can. Otherwise land downwind. A crosswind is the least favorable direction.

Look for wires first. They are hard to see and often not on the chart. Poles and a line of trees along a field edge are clues. After a forced landing, secure your wing right away, because wind can pick up an unattended canopy.

sections.heading: The power-off flare in a powered parachute
points: With no engine, you cannot add power to fix a flare that was too early. The handbook describes starting a full flare about one second before touchdown. Push both foot steering bars fully forward in one smooth motion and hold them as the rear wheels touch down. You can add more flare before landing but you cannot release it close to the ground without power.

After touchdown, release the flare smoothly and pull the canopy down. Practice with an instructor, with power on, until you can judge height and timing. A bounce or a late flare can finish with a hard landing.

sections.heading: Fire
points: Because a ram-air wing burns easily, the handbook calls an engine or fuel fire one of the most serious emergencies. The listed steps are: reduce throttle to idle, shut off the fuel if possible, shut off the magnetos, shut off all electronics, land immediately and stop as quickly as possible, and evacuate at once.
After you get out, move well away. A fuel fire can explode, and the danger reaches far from the machine.

sections.heading: Water
points: Fly over water only if you can glide to shore. The handbook says to wear a life vest for any over-water flight, carry an easy-to-reach line cutter, and practice emergency procedures.

If a water landing is certain, stay seated, turn off electronics, remove or discard objects that could trap or hurt you, tighten your belts, and pull your head, neck and legs in as you near the surface. After you hit the water, release your belts and get out. Do not go back for gear. If you are tangled in the wing lines, cut them with the line cutter.

sections.heading: Ground emergencies: wall, lock-out, lines and rollover
points: A wing wall is when the canopy forms a wall behind the cart. A lock-out is when the wing hangs back at about 45 degrees behind the cart. The handbook says that for a wall, the only safe action is to abort the takeoff and lay out the canopy again. Do not try to pop it up with sharp throttle moves, because that puts lines near the propeller. For a lock-out, it describes techniques for rectangular wings and says to ask an instructor about elliptical wings.

If lines are caught under a wheel, abort the takeoff at once. To abort, reduce the throttle, switch the magnetos off and pull the wing down. If a line is restricted by a part of the frame, you may push it clear while you keep your direction into the wind and hold RPM at kiting speed. If you cannot, shut down.

A rollover happens when the wing lifts and pulls the cart sideways. The cause is often a crosswind taxi or a takeoff before the wing is centered. If the cart is lifting on one side, reduce RPM to remove lift from the wing. If it is already tipping past recovery, turn the magnetos off, pull your arms and legs in, and do not put limbs out to stop the tip.

sections.heading: Trike tumble, ballistic parachutes and survival
points: The WSC handbook says that if a trike tumbles, structural failure and serious injury or death are likely. If the nose rotates down, push the bar out, level the wings and add full power. If the rotation keeps going and the aircraft is tumbling, deploy the ballistic parachute if one is fitted. A ballistic parachute is a rocket-launched parachute for the whole aircraft. Know where the handle is and how to arm and safe it, and keep it serviced on the maker's schedule.

After any landing away from home, make the scene safe, help anyone who is hurt and call for help. Carry a small survival kit. The handbook lists a flashlight, a signal mirror, water and food for two days, matches, a utility tool, tire repair supplies, tape for small canopy repairs and your wing bag and line sleeve. Tell someone your plan before you fly so that people know when to look.

modules.title: Training, and staying safe without a required certificate
modules.summary: Why training matters when Part 103 does not require it, what the flying associations offer, the fat ultralight problem, and the sport pilot path when your machine or your plans outgrow Part 103.
objectives: Explain why Part 103 allows flying with no training and why that is a risk.
Name the main ultralight training programs and what they are and are not.
Define the fat ultralight and explain why it is a legal and safety problem.
Describe your options when a vehicle is over the Part 103 limits.
State the minimum flight time for a sport pilot certificate in a powered parachute or a trike.
Build a personal safety plan with limits, practice and an instructor.

sections.heading: Legal freedom is not a safety record
points: Section 103.7(b) says ultralight pilots need no aeronautical knowledge, age or experience, and no airman or medical certificate. Nobody gives you a test. Nobody checks your skill or your health. AC 103-7 states that Part 103 assumes anyone who chooses to fly an ultralight has assessed the dangers and takes responsibility for his or her own safety. It says pilots should consider getting adequate training before they take part.

The same circular says that the rules protect people on the ground and other users of the airspace, and that the ultralight community is encouraged to adopt good practices to avoid more rules from the FAA. How you fly decides whether that freedom lasts.

sections.heading: Instructors and associations
points: Two national groups run training and rating programs. The United States Ultralight Association (USUA) has a Basic Flight Instructor program and says on its site that typical ultralight flight instruction runs 10 to 15 hours before the first solo. The United States Powered Paragliding Association (USPPA) has a ratings program for paramotor pilots, from PPG 1 for a student up to PPG 3 for an experienced pilot, and an instructor rating. Its page lists a minimum of 25 flights for PPG 2 and 90 flights for PPG 3.

These are association ratings. They are not FAA certificates, and nothing in Part 103 requires them. They are still worth having: they set a syllabus, give you written tests and keep you under an instructor while you are new. The USPPA page also lists suggested limits for a PPG 1 student, including a maximum wind of 8 miles per hour including gusts and flying under an instructor's supervision.

Powered parachutes, paramotors and trikes need type-specific skills: wing layout and kiting, cart handling and rollover prevention, trike pitch control, and power-off landings. A school that teaches your type is worth more than a general class.

sections.heading: Two-seat training
points: A two-seat machine cannot be a Part 103 ultralight. USUA's FAQ says that FAA exemptions allow two-seat craft for instruction only. The USPPA site also lists an FAA tandem exemption. If an instructor flies you in a two-seat machine, ask to see the exemption they are using and what it covers. Do not assume that a two-seat machine used for fun is legal under Part 103.

sections.heading: The fat ultralight problem
points: A fat ultralight is a machine that is sold, built or modified to look and be used like an ultralight, but that fails one or more of the Part 103.1 limits. It may weigh over 254 pounds empty, carry more than 5 gallons, fly faster than 55 knots, stall above 24 knots, have a second seat, or have an airworthiness certificate. Heavy engines, big tanks, electric start, instruments and enclosed seats add weight quickly.

A machine like that is not an ultralight. AC 103-7 says that any operation that does not meet every element of 103.1 is subject to all aircraft certification, pilot certification, equipment and operating rules. The pilot is responsible, as the operator, for proving the machine qualifies. A machine with provision for more than one occupant, flown alone, is still an aircraft that needs to be operated as one.

It is a safety problem as well as a legal one. A heavier, faster machine carries more energy into a crash. The pilot is flying an aircraft with no airworthiness oversight and, often, with little training. It can also create problems with insurance and with airport managers. The cure is to weigh the machine on a calibrated scale, measure the tank, check the maker's data and be honest about the result.

sections.heading: When your machine is over the limit
points: You have two choices. The first is to bring the machine within the limits. For example, replace the tank with a smaller one, using a permanent limit that the pilot cannot change in flight. AC 103-7 describes what it accepts. Do this only with the maker's advice, because changes can alter flying qualities.

The second is to fly it as an aircraft. That means registering it with an FAA N-number, getting an airworthiness certificate, keeping the operating handbook and records, and holding a pilot certificate. For powered parachutes and weight-shift trikes the usual route is the sport pilot certificate. The Powered Parachute Flying Handbook addendum from October 2025 says a powered parachute can be operated by a sport pilot with powered parachute privileges, in an aircraft that meets 14 CFR 61.316, or by a private pilot with a powered parachute rating.

MOSAIC changed the sport pilot rules in 2025. Section 61.316 now sets the performance limits and design requirements for the aircraft a sport pilot may operate. For aircraft other than airplanes the maximum stall speed in a clean configuration is 45 knots calibrated airspeed, and the seating is up to two persons. Sport pilot flight time minimums are in 61.313: 12 hours in a powered parachute, including 10 hours of flight training and 2 hours of solo, or 20 hours in a weight-shift-control aircraft, including 15 hours of training and 5 hours solo. The addendum says sport pilot applicants must hold a valid U.S. driver's license, a current third-class medical or BasicMed. Section 61.303 sets the details for using a driver's license.

sections.heading: Insurance, sites and neighbors
points: Part 103 does not require insurance, but the airport you want to use, a club or a landowner may. USUA and USPPA both advertise insurance for members. AC 103-6 reminds pilots that airport managers decide which aircraft can use their field, and that state and local laws may apply to flight parks and sites. Ask before you use any site.
Noise is the sport's greatest weakness. Fly at a reasonable height, avoid houses, livestock and horses, and use a field away from crowded places. Good neighbors keep fields open.

sections.heading: Habits that keep you alive
points: The handbook says that most powered parachute accidents come from complacency, because the aircraft is so easy to fly. Fight complacency with routine: the written checklist, written weather limits, and a standard way to start every flight. Do not let a friend or an audience push you to fly in marginal air.

Practice emergencies. Rehearse engine-out landings with an instructor, and say out loud what you will do at each altitude. Fly with an instructor again after a long break, a new wing or a new engine. Keep your flying records. After each flight, write down anything that felt odd.

Study accident reports. AC 103-6 asks pilots who see or are in an accident to take care of anyone injured, avoid moving the wreckage, write down what they remember, and tell the authorities. It also says the NTSB will investigate fatal powered ultralight accidents and other selected cases. The FAA encourages reports to the flying associations, so others can learn.

Believing an association rating is an FAA certificate. It is not.

check.q: A single-seat machine has a second seat bolted on. The owner flies it alone. What is it?
choices: An ultralight, because only one person is aboard
An aircraft, because a provision for more than one occupant takes it out of Part 103
Legal if it is under 254 pounds
check.why: AC 103-7 says that a vehicle with provision for more than one occupant can be operated only as a certificated aircraft, even with one person aboard.
